sections.skill: Use logs to check automations and prevent duplicate actions

questions.prompt: What is a log?

choices.text: A record of what an automation did and when
A list of goals that the automation hopes to achieve some time in the future

questions.correct_answer: A record of what an automation did and when
questions.intro: A LOG is a record of what an automation did and when: "9:02 sent reminder to Sam; 9:03 sent reminder to Ana." Logs let you check that it did what you expected, find errors, and explain what happened. When a step fails, automations often RETRY it. Retries are useful but risky: if the first attempt actually succeeded but the confirmation was lost, a retry can do the action TWICE, such as double-charging a card or sending a message twice. Safe designs check the log or a unique ID before repeating, so each action happens only once.

questions.prompt: Why do automations retry steps?

choices.text: Because a step may have failed
Because every step must be done exactly twice to make sure that it worked correctly

sections.skill: Compare retries with pressing an elevator button twice

questions.prompt: Why is pressing the elevator button twice harmless?

choices.text: Because pressing a button twice always cancels the first press, so nothing happens

questions.intro: Pressing an ELEVATOR button twice is harmless: the elevator still comes once. Pressing "BUY" twice on a slow website might buy two items. The difference is whether repeating changes the result. Automations retry when they are unsure a step worked. For "elevator-like" steps, that is fine. For "buy-like" steps, they must first check whether the first attempt already worked, using a record such as an order number.

sections.title: Apply it

sections.skill: Design idempotent steps and useful logs

questions.prompt: Which step is idempotent?

choices.text: "Add 10 dollars to the balance," since adding money twice is the same as adding it once

questions.intro: A design where repeating a step has the same effect as doing it once is called IDEMPOTENT. "Set the status to paid" is idempotent: doing it twice leaves it paid. "Add 10 dollars" is not: doing it twice adds 20. Logs should include enough detail (what, when, who, result) to rebuild what happened, without storing secrets such as passwords. Review logs after something goes wrong, and also spot-check them when things seem fine.
